extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners concerned with scientific language, classification, and nomenclature (philosophers of science, naturalists, taxonomists, and scientists designing terminologies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing a 'philosophical language': precise terminology, a systematic nomenclature (names for Kinds/infima species), and natural classifications that best serve induction and the discovery of laws. Includes principles about when language should be mechanical (as in algebra) and when it must resist mechanical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology suited for precision
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminology suited for describing with precision the individual facts observed (one of the essential parts of a philosophical language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology should allow precise description of observed particulars. It is one of the principal requisites of a philosophical language alongside completeness (nomenclature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Name for every common property
rubrics_metrics.description: A name for every common property of any importance or interest detected by comparing facts, including concrete names for the classes we artificially construct in virtue of those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There should be names for properties we frequently predicate; these names enable concise expression and facilitate memory and thought (e.g., inventing or selecting suitable names to mark distinctions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature: name for every Kind (infima species)
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be a name for every Kind—i.e., for every lowest Kind or infima species with which any branch of knowledge is conversant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A systematic nomenclature assigns names to the lowest Kinds; when new lowest Kinds are discovered, names should be given on a uniform principle (examples: Linnæan taxonomy and modern chemical nomenclature). Lack of systematic nomenclature (e.g., mineralogy) retards scientific progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish nomenclature from terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomenclature (names of Kinds) and terminology (descriptive expressions for properties) are distinct and should be treated differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'nomenclature' for systematic naming of Kinds (e.g., 'Viola odorata') and 'terminology' for descriptive terms (e.g., 'serrated', 'dentate'). The reform in chemistry is a nomenclature change, not a new terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic and uniform assignment of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomenclature should be constructed on a system so that new species get names at once on a uniform principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic formation prevents confusion and supports rapid incorporation of discoveries; contrast with domains where no system exists and progress is hindered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation of names in nomenclature includes 'Kind'hood
rubrics_metrics.description: Words belonging to a nomenclature connote both certain attributes and that those attributes are distinctive of a Kind (i.e., they connote that the class is a Kind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'peroxide of iron' connotes being a compound of iron and a maximal dose of oxygen and that this composition is a peculiar Kind. The form of a name indicates it is to denote an infima species, and the connoted descriptive characters are part of its meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning unfolded by definition plus form of word
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of characters employed to discriminate each Kind (a real definition) together with the form of the nomenclatural word constitutes the whole meaning of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions enumerate distinguishing characters; the form of the name (indicating Kind status) and the definition together unfold signification. If characters change as better diagnostics are chosen, the connotation/definition may be reformed while keeping denotation stable where desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal requisites: precision (definiteness) and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The two principal requisites of a philosophical language are precision (definiteness) and completeness; nomenclature (names for Kinds) is the third main component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision helps in unambiguous predication; completeness requires adequate coverage of terms and names for the needed kinds of subjects. Secondary qualities (e.g., aphorisms by Whewell) exist but are less central here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make language mechanical when safe; resist mechanical use otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the nature of the subject permits reasoning to be carried on mechanically, the language should be constructed on as mechanical principles as possible; otherwise it should be constructed to create obstacles to merely mechanical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebra exemplifies ideal mechanical language for number relations. But for subjects not reducible to purely mechanical procedures, language should prevent mindless symbol manipulation and keep users conscious of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating non-mathematical scientific language like algebraic symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic notation is perfect for the purposes of numerical relations but is a poor universal model; using names as unmeaning counters is only appropriate for a narrow class of deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-mathematical sciences, reasoning requires a distinct mental image of phenomena; reducing everything to symbol manipulation leads to loss of necessary attention to particulars and to errors when other laws intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain and encode meaning in word-formation (derivation and analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: As much meaning as possible should be thrown into the formation of the word itself; derivation and analogy should be used to keep alive consciousness of what is signified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages that form compounds and derivatives from native roots and by fixed analogies (e.g., German, Greek) have advantages. English/French/Italian, relying on foreign/dead roots, are less helpful for keeping meaning evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuously revive word-meanings through engagement with phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Because words tend to lose their vivid meaning by use, the only possible mode of reviving meaning is continual 'stamping' of them by living in habitual contemplation of the phenomena themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not live only among formulas and technical rules; habitual attention to realities prevent progressive loss of meaning and misapplication of formulæ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as contrivance to order ideas for memory and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is a contrivance for the best possible ordering of the ideas of objects in our minds to give greatest command over knowledge acquired and to lead directly to acquiring more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal: group things so that ideas follow one another to maximize remembrance and ascertainment of laws. Classification here is subsidiary to induction and focused on real objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select classificatory properties that are causes or sure marks of many other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties chosen as foundations for classification should, if possible, be those which are causes of many other properties, or at least sure marks of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer causal or reliably indicative properties because they yield many further general propositions. Artificial choices (e.g., Linnæan stamens/pistils) that produce groups with few shared important propositions are less useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for classifications supporting many and important general propositions (natural classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific (natural) classification should form groups respecting which a greater number of general propositions can be made, and those propositions be more important, than for other groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural classification tends to place objects similar in general aspect together because such grouping often corresponds to many shared properties. Natural does not mean necessarily obvious properties; importance matters more than obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using unobvious foundational properties, provide recognizable marks for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: When a natural classification is founded on unobvious but important properties, there must be other properties more readily recognizable that co-exist and can serve as marks of the fundamental properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: zoological classification should be founded on internal structure but must use external integuments or other observable marks so species can be determined without destructive methods (De Blainville's preference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitute classes with reference to all existing objects (systematic placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot properly constitute any class except in reference to a general division of the whole of nature; determining the place of objects requires considering all varieties of existing objects with any degree of affinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A family or genus must be formed as part of a systematic arrangement of the whole domain (e.g., plants/animals) so that class boundaries are rational and informed by overall affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications must conform to the purpose/ends in view
rubrics_metrics.description: The properties according to which objects are classified should relate to the particular end in view; different sciences or practical ends justify different classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: farmers classify plants into useful vs weeds; geologists classify fossils by strata/period; whales may be called fish for whaling purposes but not for physiology. Multiple valid classifications can coexist depending on purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good classification facilitates mutual improvement of knowledge and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A good classification draws attention to the properties on which it is founded and facilitates the discovery of other properties, so that knowledge of things and their classification mutually improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By grouping objects on informative properties, classification directs inquiry to look for correlated attributes and thus aids progressive refinement of both knowledge and classificatory schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that natural groups may be given by 'Type' not by strict definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural groups may be 'given by Type, not by Definition'—their descriptions are often loose, admit anomalies, and state what happens usually rather than invariably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect indefiniteness and anomalies in natural groups (e.g., Rosaceae with genera lacking typical characters). Diagnostic/artificial characters may be imperfect and yield to broader natural affinities; classification must accommodate such irregularities.
